description:
Interested in wildfire monitoring and NASA Earth data? Harmonize MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data. 

Contribute: build Python/data-processing pipelines; work with GIS and satellite data; develop visualization or web tools; apply ML/statistics; design the user experience; or craft the story and impact.
summary:
The **Wildfire Intelligence Platform** is a high-performance geospatial web application built with Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, OpenStreetMap, and Uber’s H3 Spatial Indexing system to analyze and visualize wildfire risk.

Anchored at a continental datum with live OpenStreetMap tile streaming, the interactive canvas lets users click anywhere on Earth to instantly compute Resolution 9 H3 hexagons and contiguous neighbor autocorrelation polygons. It integrates Nominatim geocoding for address searches, coordinate lookups, and GPS geolocation, alongside pre-calibrated study zones across high-risk terrains like the Diablo Range, Santa Cruz Mountains, and Paradise fire scar.

For life-safety operational warnings, Pyros H3 utilizes a rare-event decision framework balancing accuracy-optimal and precision-optimal thresholds. An interactive boundary scrubber provides live feedback on confusion matrices, precision, and recall curves, triggering automatic alerts when thresholds diverge.

The platform synthesizes multi-source telemetry—including GridMET atmospheric vectors, NASA satellite soil moisture and evaporative stress, USGS elevation slopes, and OpenStreetMap infrastructure proximity—alongside real-time scenario controls and one-click JSON export. Designed with Overpass, Fira Sans, and JetBrains Mono typography, its interface avoids emojis and blue-purple gradients in favor of calibrated telemetry slates, ochres, ambers, and deep embers.
details:
The problem

Wildfire risk models built at county resolution have a structural flaw: they average away the exact heterogeneity that determines whether a fire ignites and spreads. Santa Clara County contains the fog-cooled, moisture-retaining Santa Cruz Mountains and the hot, wind-exposed Diablo Range in the same administrative boundary; treating them as one number erases the difference that actually matters. A related, quieter problem shows up in how these models get built and validated: it's easy to simulate data from an invented formula, fit a model back to that same simulated data, and mistake "the model recovered the coefficients I put in" for "the model discovered something true about wildfire physics." Add to that the fact that ignitions are rare events, often well under 5% of any given cell-day and a model that's graded on plain classification accuracy will look great by simply predicting "no fire" everywhere, while being operationally useless as a warning system.

This backend was built to close those three gaps at once: replace county-wide lumping with per-location prediction, replace invented ground truth with real measured data, and replace a single "accuracy" number with an evaluation framework that actually accounts for how rare and costly a missed ignition is.

What NASA data it runs on

Two NASA Earth-science products, both published through the data.nasa.gov open data catalog, supply the fuel-moisture signal that was previously just a hand-picked coefficient:

  • ECOSTRESS Evaporative Stress Index (ECO_L4G_ESI.002) - a 70-meter-resolution measurement of how hard vegetation is transpiring relative to its potential. When plants pull back on transpiration because they're water-stressed, ESI drops, and that drop is a real, physically grounded signal of vegetation dryness - not a guess.
  • SMAP L4 Global Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP.007) - a NASA/JPL model-assimilated product giving continuous surface and root-zone soil moisture at 9-kilometer resolution, refreshed every three hours. It fills in exactly the "fuel moisture" input the earlier version of this system was missing.

Both are pulled through AppEEARS, NASA's authenticated point-sampling API, so a request for one coordinate and one date returns real satellite/model-derived values rather than a number typed into a config file. A third NASA product, the MODIS/VIIRS burned-area record (MCD64A1), is the intended source of training labels - actual historical burn dates per pixel, replacing what had been a coin-flip generated from an assumed formula.

What the backend actually does

Every prediction is anchored to a fine-grained H3 hexagon (roughly a tenth of a square kilometer) rather than a county or a hand-drawn zone, so a query for a point in the Santa Cruz Mountains and a query for a point in the Diablo Range pull genuinely different terrain, weather, and moisture values instead of sharing one blended number. For a given latitude, longitude, and date, it assembles a feature vector - atmospheric dryness from GridMET, real vegetation and soil moisture from ECOSTRESS and SMAP L4, terrain from a USGS elevation model, and distance to roads and power lines from OpenStreetMap - and feeds it into one joint gradient-boosted model, rather than four separately-fit models for fuel, weather, terrain, and human factors that would each suffer from ignoring the others.

The model itself is trained with spatial block cross-validation, so a fire's neighboring pixels can't leak between the training and test sets the way a naive random split would allow. Its output isn't a single risk score with one implicit threshold; it's a calibrated probability paired with two different decision points computed from held-out data — one tuned to maximize overall accuracy, one tuned to maximize precision without missing too many real ignitions. Because rare-event base rates push those two optimal thresholds apart, the system compares them and only surfaces the accuracy-vs-precision toggle to a user when they actually disagree by a meaningful margin, rather than showing a choice that wouldn't change anything.

The result is a /predict endpoint that, given a location and date, returns a real per-cell fire risk probability, both operating points, and a transparent snapshot of every covariate that went into the answer - so nothing in the output is a coefficient nobody can trace back to a measurement.
